catalog_quote: For instance, in Ɛsahie, the word [bɔkɔ:] has two meanings depending on the type of tone pattern used in the production of the word. It can be produced with a low- low tone, or a high- high tone to convey different meanings. This is seen in example (5.1) below. Example 5.1. a. bɔ́kɔ́: ‘completely’ b. bɔ̀kɔ̀: ‘slowly’ The examples show that like most tonal languages, the meaning of a word in Ɛsahie does not depend on the segments alone, but also on the pitch patterns associated with them. [...] In Ɛsahie, monomoraic and bimoraic syllable can carry tones of the same value, also every vowel constitutes a syllable, and pre-consonantal nasals are syllabic. Multiple tones cannot be assigned to a syllable, and toneless segments are usually associated with the tone of the next syllable. We therefore conclude the TBU in Ɛsahie to be the syllable. new_statements.rule_in_words: Ɛsahie is a two-tone (H/L) register-tone language with the syllable as tone-bearing unit; lexical tone distinguishes words and grammatical tone marks TAM on verbs. The only full phonology of the language (Ansah 2019) and every other description are silent on word stress; the nearest explicit remark is Broohm & Melloni 2020: 37, who characterise Kwa languages including Esahie as having 'a tone (non-stress) based phonological system'.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal detail: three tonal classes for basic nouns (L, LH, H) and three for basic verbs; nominal suffixes trigger tone change while prefixes do not; TAM changes the tone melody without segmental change (Ansah 2019 abstract, pp. 176-249). English loanwords adapt segmentally (§4.5) — the thesis does not say how English stress maps onto Ɛsahie tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word), elicited citation forms of nouns and verbs plus inflected forms, from fieldwork in Sehwi towns and written Ɛsahie texts. Broohm 2014 fn. 1 adds that information structure is not encoded prosodically.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Esahie/Ɛsahie = Sehwi [sfw], glottocode sehw1238 (Glottolog lists no dialect codes). Broohm 2019 states his consultants were all speakers of the Wiawso (southern) variety; Ansah 2019's fieldwork towns are not specified in the parts read, and she treats the language as one. The two named dialects (Wiawso, Anhwiaso) differ lexically and are mutually intelligible.

sources.note: Full phonology (segments, syllable, tone). Ch. 5 'Tone and tonal processes' (pp. 171-249): Ɛsahie is a tonal language with H and L, three tonal classes of basic nouns and of basic verbs, TBU = syllable (pp. 175-176). The word 'stress' occurs only for English loanword sources (4.5.1.4 'Unstressed vowel replacement', p. 159, about English /ʌ, ə/). No statement on word stress or prominence in Ɛsahie itself.

sources.note: p. 37: Kwa languages 'have a tone (non-stress) based phonological system, and where both tone and processual morphology are deployed in AN construction' (contrasting with English stress alternation); p. 49 (4.1): 'Like Akan, Esahie is a tonal language that distinguishes between two basic contrastive tones' (bó 'beat' / bò 'buttocks'). Closest thing to an explicit no-stress statement, but framed at the Kwa level.
